Il ferro accorcia il T2*: nelle sequenze: Iron shortens T2*: in multi-echo gradient-echo sequences the signal of iron-loaded tissue falls faster the more iron there is. You draw an ROI and fit a curve S(TE) = S0·e^(−TE/T2*); R2* = 1000/T2* (s⁻¹). Heart: full-thickness ROI on the interventricular septum of the mid-ventricular short-axis slice (away from the susceptibility artifacts of the cardiac veins and lung in the lateral wall). Cardiac thresholds at 1.5 T: T2* > 20 ms normal, 10-20 ms mild-moderate overload, < 10 ms severe. Liver: ROI in the right-lobe parenchyma away from vessels; the liver iron concentration (LIC, mg Fe/g dry weight) is estimated from R2* with a calibration curve (the collection uses Garbowski 2014: LIC ≈ 0.029·R2*^1.014). Most used LIC classes: < 2 mg/g normal (up to about 1.8), 2-7 mild, 7-15 moderate, > 15 severe. With very low signal, noise creates a «floor»: a fit on all echoes overestimates T2*; truncation of the late echoes or a model with a constant (offset) is used. In the viewer, the T2* tool (More measurements → T2*) copies the ROI to all echoes of the slice, shows the curve, T2* and R2* with both models and, for the liver, the LIC. In this girl the myocardium does not lose signal appreciably over the echoes (collection T2* 29.6 ms, normal), while the liver is almost black from the fourth echo (T2* 2.0 ms, R2* 500 s⁻¹, LIC about 16 mg/g: severe). In children transfusional iron deposits first in the liver; the heart usually loads later, but it must be checked periodically with MRI. In small hearts the septum is thin: zoom in before drawing the ROI and keep it in the myocardium, even if only a few pixels, because cavity blood has a long T2* and raises the value (an ROI that includes blood gives values above 100-200 ms with the T2* tool).
